“Well, you young rascal,” the old lady cried as he came into the room, “why haven’t you visited me all this time?”

“My dear Lady Clem, I never get a moment to myself,” Lord Arthur said with a smile.

“I suppose that means you spend all day with Miss Sybil Merton, buying pretty things and talking nonsense? I can’t understand why people make such a fuss over getting married. In my day we never dreamed of making love to each other in public, or in private either, for that matter.”

“I promise I haven’t seen Sybil for twenty-four hours, Lady Clem. From what I can tell, the hatmakers have taken complete possession of her.”

“Of course. That’s the only reason you visit an ugly old woman like me. I wonder why you men never learn. Men have done foolish things for my sake, and here I am now, a poor creature with aching joints, false hair, and a bad temper. Without dear Lady Jansen, who sends me the most scandalous French novels she can find, I don’t think I could get through the day. Doctors are good for nothing except taking your money. They can’t even cure my heartburn.”

“I’ve brought you something to cure it, Lady Clem,” Lord Arthur said seriously. “It’s a wonderful invention by an American.”

“I don’t think I like American inventions, Arthur. In fact, I’m quite sure I don’t. I read some American novels recently, and they were absolute nonsense.”

“But there’s nothing nonsensical about this, Lady Clem! I promise it’s a perfect cure. You must agree to try it.” Lord Arthur took the little box from his pocket and gave it to her.

“Well, what a lovely box, Arthur. Is it really a gift? How sweet of you. And is this the wonderful medicine? It looks like a sweet. I’ll take it straight away.”

“Good heavens, Lady Clem!” Lord Arthur exclaimed, seizing her hand. “You mustn’t do that. It’s a homeopathic medicine, and taking it when you haven’t got heartburn could do you terrible harm. Wait for an attack and take it then. You’ll be amazed by the result.”

“I’d like to take it now,” Lady Clementina said, lifting the small clear capsule toward the light. A bubble of liquid aconitine floated inside. “I’m certain it tastes delicious. The truth is, although I hate doctors, I love medicine. Still, I’ll save it for my next attack.”

“And when will that happen?” Lord Arthur asked eagerly.

Jane admitted to some surprise at the engagement; yet she spoke less of her astonishment than of her fervent wish for their happiness, and Elizabeth could not induce her to think that happiness unlikely. Kitty and Lydia felt no envy whatever of Miss Lucas, since Mr. Collins was merely a clergyman. To them the affair meant nothing beyond a fresh piece of news to circulate in Meryton.

Lady Lucas could scarcely fail to feel triumphant at being able to return Mrs. Bennet’s boasts with the satisfaction of having a daughter suitably married. She visited Longbourn somewhat more frequently than usual to declare her pleasure, though Mrs. Bennet’s displeased countenance and unkind observations might have sufficed to banish happiness itself.

A reserve between Elizabeth and Charlotte prevented either from speaking of the matter, and Elizabeth believed that true confidence could never exist between them again. Disappointment in Charlotte turned her with increased affection towards her sister. Her judgment of Jane’s integrity and delicacy, she was certain, could never alter; and her anxiety for Jane’s happiness increased each day, for Bingley had now been absent a week without any report of his return.

Jane had answered Caroline’s letter promptly, and was reckoning the days until she could reasonably expect another. On Tuesday the promised letter of gratitude from Mr. Collins reached their father, expressed with all the solemn thankfulness that a year’s residence with the family might have warranted. Having satisfied his conscience upon this point, he went on, in many ecstatic phrases, to acquaint them with his joy at winning the affection of their amiable neighbour, Miss Lucas. He next explained that the sole reason for his ready acceptance of their kind desire to welcome him again at Longbourn was the prospect of enjoying her company. He hoped to return there on Monday fortnight; Lady Catherine, he further remarked, approved his marriage so warmly that she desired it to be celebrated with the least possible delay. This, he trusted, would supply an argument his dear Charlotte could not answer against fixing an early date to make him the happiest of men.

The prospect of Mr. Collins coming back to Hertfordshire no longer afforded Mrs. Bennet pleasure. Indeed, she was quite as ready to grumble about it as her husband. How odd that he should choose Longbourn rather than Lucas Lodge; and how inconvenient and excessively troublesome it would be. She detested entertaining visitors while her health remained so poor, and people in love were the most disagreeable guests of all.

I was sorry to hear Jim say that; it made me think less of him. My conscience started tormenting me worse than ever, until finally I told it, “Give me a break—it isn’t too late yet. I’ll paddle to shore at the first light I see and tell someone.” Right away I felt comfortable and happy, light as a feather. Every worry was gone. I kept a sharp lookout for a light, singing a little to myself. After a while one appeared. Jim called out:

“We’re safe, Huck, we’re safe! Jump up and kick your heels! That’s good old Cairo at last, I just know it!”

I said:

“I’ll take the canoe and find out, Jim. You know, it might be somewhere else.”

He sprang up and got the canoe ready, laid his old coat in the bottom for me to sit on, and handed me the paddle. As I pushed away, he said:

“Pretty soon I’ll be shouting for joy, and I’ll say it’s all because of Huck. I’m a free man, and I never could’ve been free without Huck; Huck made it happen. Jim will never forget you, Huck. You’re the best friend Jim ever had, and you’re the only friend old Jim has now.”

I was paddling off, sweating with eagerness to report him. But those words seemed to knock all the strength out of me. I moved more slowly after that, no longer sure whether I was pleased I’d set out or not. When I was fifty yards away, Jim called:

“There you go, good old faithful Huck, the only white gentleman who ever kept his promise to old Jim.”

Well, I felt sick. But I told myself I had to do it; there was no getting out of it. Just then a small boat came along carrying two men with guns. They stopped, and so did I. One asked:

“What’s that over there?”

“A section of a raft,” I said.

“Is that where you belong?”

“Yes, sir.”

“Any men aboard?”

“Just one, sir.”

“Well, five black slaves ran away tonight up there, above the bend. Is your man white or black?”

I couldn’t answer at once. I tried, but nothing came out. For a second or two I tried to gather my courage and say it, but I wasn’t man enough—I had less nerve than a rabbit. I could feel myself giving way, so I stopped trying and said:

“He’s white.”

“I guess we’ll have a look ourselves.”

“I wish you would,” I said, “because it’s my father over there, and maybe you could help me tow the raft to shore where that light is.”
